statement: The input is the bytes before its first NUL byte; anything after it is ignored.
A backslash followed by `n` (0x6E) becomes one newline byte (0x0A).
A backslash followed by any byte other than `n` becomes one backslash, and that byte is dropped. In particular `\\` becomes `\`, `\t` becomes `\` and `\N` becomes `\`.
A backslash that is the last byte of the input stays a backslash.
Every byte that is not part of an escape is copied unchanged, including control bytes and bytes 0x80 to 0xFF.
Escapes do not chain: the input is scanned once, left to right, and the output is never re-scanned. `\\n` becomes `\n` (two bytes, backslash and `n`).
The output is never longer than the input.
A version 6 statement operand is a signed 16-bit value, so a statement can name global slots 0 to 32767 only (PROGS-7.2); a program with more globals cannot reach the rest from code.
A definition's `ofs` is unsigned 16-bit, so a definition can name global or field slots 0 to 65535 (PROGS-9.2).
A definition's type has 15 bits once `DEF_SAVEGLOBAL` is removed: 0 to 32767.

A function has at most 8 parameters (`parm_size` has 8 entries and the call opcodes are `OP_CALL0` to `OP_CALL8`). Each parameter has 3 slots in the call area (PROGS-18.1), and qcc writes a `parm_size` of 1 or 3; the engine copies whatever `parm_size` says without checking it.

Entering a QC function adds one to the call depth, and the entry that makes the depth reach 32 fails with `stack overflow`. The function the engine calls counts, so at most 31 QC functions can be active at once.
The depth is shared by every QC function active in the engine, including those started by a nested `PR_ExecuteProgram` (for example a touch function run from inside a builtin).
Builtins do not count: calling a builtin does not enter a QC frame.

Entering a QC function saves its `locals` slots on a stack of 2048 slots shared by all active functions. An entry is allowed when the slots in use plus the new function's `locals` is at most 2048, and fails with `PR_ExecuteProgram: locals stack overflow` when it is more.

Each call of `PR_ExecuteProgram` has its own counter starting at 100000. The counter drops by one before each statement, and the statement that brings it to 0 fails with `runaway loop error` without executing, so one call executes at most 99999 statements.
Statements run by a nested `PR_ExecuteProgram` count against the nested call's own counter, not the outer one.
id's builtin table has 79 entries, numbers 0 to 78. Calling a function whose builtin number is 79 or more fails with `Bad builtin call number`.
Builtin 0 cannot be called: a `first_statement` of 0 is not negative, so the function runs statement 0 instead (PROGS-10.2).
A `first_statement` of -2147483648 has no positive builtin number; negating it overflows, which is undefined in C. This spec fixes the answer as `Bad builtin call number`.

A server has at most 600 edicts, counting the world and the client edicts. When none can be reused and 600 are in use, allocating one (`spawn`, or an entity of the map being loaded) fails with `ED_Alloc: no free edicts`. Reuse rules are in `edicts.md` (P1-03).

The sound and model precache lists have 256 entries each, and entry 0 is always the empty string. Precaching a name already in the list does nothing; precaching a new name when all 256 entries are used fails with `PF_precache_sound: overflow` or `PF_precache_model: overflow`. So at most 255 sounds can be precached, and at most 255 models including the world model in entry 1 and its submodels after it.

qcc never checks its table sizes: more than 500000 bytes of strings, 65536 statements, 8192 functions, 16384 global definitions, 1024 field definitions or 16384 global slots overruns a fixed array, which is undefined in C. The result is not specified; a program that exceeds one does not build reliably with id's qcc.
A name of 63 or more characters fails with `name too long`, so a name has at most 62 characters.

qcc records the files named in `precache_sound`, `precache_model` and `precache_file` calls, 1024 of each. A new sound when 1024 are recorded fails with `PrecacheSound: numsounds == MAX_SOUNDS`, and a new file when 1024 are recorded with `PrecacheFile: numfiles == MAX_FILES`. For models qcc tests the sound count instead (`PrecacheModels: numsounds == MAX_SOUNDS`), so a new model fails only when 1024 sounds are recorded, and the 1025th model overruns its array.
Every multi-byte integer and float in the file is little-endian. The engine converts with `LittleLong` and `LittleShort` after loading, so a big-endian host reads the same values.

The file starts with the 60-byte header (PROGS-2) at offset 0. Each of the six tables (statements, global definitions, field definitions, functions, strings, globals) is located only by its offset and count in the header; the engine does not require any order, alignment, gap or absence of overlap between them.

id's qcc writes the tables in this order, each directly after the previous one: header, strings, statements, functions, global definitions, field definitions, globals. It pads the string table with NUL bytes to a multiple of 4, so every table starts 4-byte aligned.
Bytes in the file that no table covers are ignored, except by the file CRC (PROGS-6.1).

The first record of the statements, functions, global definitions and field definitions tables, and the first byte of the string table, are reserved: qcc writes them as all zero bytes (`InitData` starts every count at 1). The engine does not check them.
The header is 15 consecutive `i32` fields, 60 bytes:

Every offset is measured from the first byte of the file. A table occupies `count * record size` bytes from its offset; for the string table the count is already in bytes and for the globals the record size is 4.
The fields are signed in id's struct. The engine never compares an offset or a count with the file size and never checks a sign; a reader's checks are in PROGS-15.
A file whose `version` is not 6 is rejected with `progs.dat has wrong version number (<version> should be 6)`.
A file whose `crc` is not 5927 is rejected with `progs.dat system vars have been modified, progdefs.h is out of date`.
The version is checked before the CRC: a file wrong in both reports the version.
A field definition whose `type` has bit 15 (`DEF_SAVEGLOBAL`) set is rejected with `PR_LoadProgs: pr_fielddefs[i].type & DEF_SAVEGLOBAL`. The same bit in a global definition is accepted (PROGS-9.3).

These three are the only checks the engine makes on a loaded file; it does not check offsets, counts, string references, opcodes or operands at load. A missing file is rejected with `PR_LoadProgs: couldn't load progs.dat`.

The header CRC identifies the system globals and fields a mod declares (PROGS-5), not the file: two different mods with the same system definitions carry the same value, 5927 for the definitions in id's `defs.qc`.

The CRC is the 16-bit, non-reflected CRC with polynomial 0x1021, initial value 0xFFFF and final XOR 0x0000 (CRC-16/CCITT-FALSE). Each byte updates it as `crc = (crc << 8) ^ table[(crc >> 8) ^ byte]`, truncated to 16 bits, where `table[i]` is the CRC of the single byte `i` with a zero initial value.
The CRC of no bytes is 0xFFFF (65535), and the CRC of the ASCII bytes `123456789` is 0x29B1.
The header `crc` is PROGS-4's CRC of exactly that text, with `\n` as one byte 0x0A. For `WinQuake/progdefs.q1` it is 5927.
qcc stores the CRC zero-extended from 16 bits, so the field is between 0 and 65535 in any file id's qcc writes.
While loading, the engine also computes PROGS-4's CRC over every byte of the file as stored, before any byte swapping, into `pr_crc`.
`pr_crc` is never checked. Its only use is the server info message, which prints it as `VERSION <version> SERVER (<pr_crc> CRC)`.
A statement is 8 bytes:

The operands are signed 16-bit: the bytes `ff ff` are -1, not 65535. Most opcodes use an operand as a global slot index; `OP_GOTO` uses `a`, and `OP_IF` and `OP_IFNOT` use `b`, as a jump relative to the statement. Their meaning per opcode is in `vm.md`.
Statement 0 is reserved (PROGS-1.5); a function's code starts at `first_statement` (PROGS-10) and the table has no other structure.
The engine does not check `op` or the operands at load. An opcode above `OP_BITOR` (65) fails only when executed, with `Bad opcode <op>`.
The vanilla opcodes are numbered from 0 in this order, 66 in all (0 to 65):
A definition is 8 bytes:
`ofs` is unsigned: a definition can name any slot from 0 to 65535, unlike a statement operand (PROGS-7.2).

In a global definition, `DEF_SAVEGLOBAL` marks a global that a saved game stores. qcc sets it on every global that has no initial value, is not a function or field, and is not a local or parameter. The engine strips the bit before using the type.
Several definitions can name the same slot: qcc gives a vector `v` the definitions `v` (vector) and `v_x` (float) at the same slot, and `v_y` and `v_z` at the next two.

For a field `.T name`, qcc writes a field definition with type `T` at the field's slot, and a global definition with type field (5) for a global slot whose value is that field slot index. A vector field also gets `name_x`, `name_y` and `name_z` field definitions and globals for its three slots.
Lookups by name compare bytes exactly (`strcmp`) and take the first matching definition in table order; lookups by slot take the first definition whose `ofs` matches.

qcc also writes global definitions for the parameters and locals of functions, without `DEF_SAVEGLOBAL`, and one named `IMMEDIATE` for every constant slot it allocates (string, float and vector literals), so names in the table are not unique.
A function is 36 bytes:

A function with `first_statement` below zero is builtin number `-first_statement`; qcc writes `#25` as -25. The engine calls the builtin without reading `parm_start`, `locals`, `numparms` or `parm_size`.
A global of type function holds an index into this table, and index 0 is the null function: calling it fails with `NULL function`.
`parm_size` is eight single bytes and is not byte-swapped; entries at or past `numparms` are ignored (qcc writes them as 0).

`numparms` below zero copies no parameters; qcc writes -1 for a function declared with `...`. qcc does not limit the count to 8, but the engine reads only `parm_size[0..numparms)`, so a reader rejects more than 8 (PROGS-15.6).
The engine does not interpret `profile` at load; it adds one for every statement the function executes, starting from the stored value. qcc writes 0.

The string table is `numstrings` bytes holding NUL-terminated strings. A string reference (`s_name`, `s_file`, or the value of a string global) is a byte offset from the start of the table, and the string runs to the next NUL byte.
Offset 0 is the empty string: qcc writes a NUL as the first byte.

A reference may point into the middle of another string; the string is the bytes from that offset to the next NUL. qcc's `CopyString` appends every string it is given without looking for an earlier copy, so the same text can appear several times.
The bytes are uninterpreted: any value from 0x01 to 0xFF can be part of a string, including control characters and Quake's high-bit characters.
The table ends with zero to three NUL padding bytes from qcc (PROGS-1.3).

At run time a string value can also point outside the table, at strings the engine allocates (`ED_NewString`, `sv.name`); those values are still offsets from the start of the table and never appear in a file as written by qcc.

The globals are `numglobals` 4-byte slots holding the initial value of every global, constant and temporary. The engine executes in this memory directly, so the values in the file are the state before the first function runs.
A slot holds whichever type the code using it says (PROGS-17): the file does not tag slots with types, and only the definitions (PROGS-9) say what a named slot holds.
Slots 0 to 27 are the reserved return and parameter area (PROGS-18). qcc allocates every other global from slot 28 upward, so a file from qcc has at least 28 slots.
`entityfields` is the number of 4-byte field slots in every entity. The engine sizes each edict as `entityfields * 4` bytes of fields plus its own fixed header.
qcc counts one slot per non-vector field and three per vector field, in declaration order; a field's slot index is the count before it.
The engine does not check `entityfields` against the field definitions; `edicts.md` (P1-03) covers the system fields that must come first.
Loading a file that passes PROGS-3 yields every field of every record exactly as stored, after the little-endian conversion of PROGS-1.1; the loader changes no value.
Loading has no other effect on the file's contents: the tables keep their counts, order and duplicates, and the reserved first records stay as stored.
A file shorter than the 60-byte header is rejected.
A table whose offset or count is negative, or whose end (`offset + count * record size`) is past the end of the file, is rejected. The end is computed without overflow.
A string reference in a definition (`s_name`) or a function (`s_name`, `s_file`) that is negative or not less than `numstrings` is rejected.

A string reference whose bytes reach the end of the string table without a NUL is rejected. (id's engine would read on into the next table, or into the NUL that `COM_LoadFile` appends after the last byte of the file.)

A file is checked in this order and the first failure is reported: size, then version (PROGS-3.1), then header CRC (PROGS-3.2), then table bounds, then field definition flags (PROGS-3.4), then string references, then function parameter counts.
A function whose `numparms` is greater than 8 is rejected.

Statement opcodes and operands, function `first_statement`, `parm_start` and `locals`, definition `ofs`, and the values of globals are not checked at load, as in id's engine: what an out-of-range value does when executed is in `vm.md`.
A reader may skip the header CRC check (PROGS-3.2) when asked to, so the editor can open a mod whose system definitions differ from id's; the default is to check.
The type numbers used in definitions (PROGS-9.1) are:

The slot counts are id's `type_size` table. The engine computes the pointer's size as `sizeof(void *)/4`, which is 1 on the 32-bit x86 build id shipped and 2 on a 64-bit build; this spec fixes 1, the value of the shipped engine and of qcc's own table (`{1,1,1,3,1,1,1,1}`).

A definition type above 7 (after removing `DEF_SAVEGLOBAL`) is not a vanilla type. id's engine has no check for it and prints such a value as `bad type <n>`; a reader keeps the number rather than rejecting the file.
QuakeC has no way to declare a pointer: `ev_pointer` values exist only at run time, made by `OP_ADDRESS`, and qcc writes no definition of type 7.
A slot is 4 bytes read either as an f32 or as an i32; the engine reinterprets the same bits (`eval_t` is a union) and never converts between them when copying.
A string value is an i32 byte offset from the start of the string table (PROGS-11); 0 is the empty string.
A float value is the f32 in the slot; a vector is three consecutive float slots, x first.

An entity value is an i32 byte offset from the start of the engine's edict array, which is the entity number times the engine's edict size, not the entity number; 0 is the world. The file never holds a non-zero entity value, since QuakeC cannot initialise one.
A field value is an i32 slot index into an entity's fields (PROGS-13), so `.origin_y` is one more than `.origin`.
A function value is an i32 index into the functions table (PROGS-10); 0 is the null function.
A pointer value is an i32 byte offset from the start of the engine's edict array to one field slot of one entity.

Slot 0 is `OFS_NULL`; slots 1 to 3 hold a function's return value (`OFS_RETURN`, three slots so a vector fits); slots 4 to 27 hold the eight call parameters, three slots each, parameter `n` at `4 + 3n`.
Slots 0 to 27 have no global definitions in a file from qcc, and the system globals start at slot 28, which is why `progdefs.h` opens with `int pad[28]` (PROGS-5.1).
A version 7 file has a 92-byte header: the 60 bytes of PROGS-2, then eight more 4-byte fields:
`secondaryversion` 0x021B1461 (`"1FTE" ^ "PROG"` as little-endian i32) means the 16-bit layout of PROGS-7 and PROGS-9; 0x65167402 (`"1FTE" ^ "32B "`) means the 32-bit layout of PROGS-20.
FTE also accepts version 7 with `secondaryversion` `"UH27"` or `"KKQW"`, or any other value (treated as KKQWSV's format). Those are other engines' layouts; a reader rejects them as unsupported.
In FTE's header the offsets and counts are unsigned, but they are bounded by the file size, so PROGS-15.2 applies unchanged.
In the 16-bit layout FTE declares statement operands unsigned (`dstatement16_t`), so in a version 7 file the bytes `ff ff` are operand 65535. This differs from PROGS-7.2, which holds for version 6.
In the 32-bit layout a statement is 16 bytes: `op`, `a`, `b` and `c`, each a u32, at offsets 0, 4, 8 and 12.
In the 32-bit layout a definition is 12 bytes: `type` u32 at 0, `ofs` u32 at 4 and `s_name` i32 at 8. `DEF_SAVEGLOBAL` is still bit 15 of `type`.
Functions, strings and globals keep the layout of PROGS-10 to PROGS-12.
When `ofslinenums` is not 0, it is the offset of `numstatements` i32 source line numbers, one per statement in statement order.
The bodyless function table is `numbodylessfuncs` NUL-terminated names stored one after another from `ofsbodylessfuncs`.

Bit `n` of `blockscompressed` set means a table is stored compressed: bit 0 statements, 1 global definitions, 2 field definitions, 3 functions, 4 strings, 5 globals, 6 line numbers, 7 types. A compressed table starts at its offset with an i32 compressed length followed by that many bytes of zlib data (`QC_decode` method 2).

A reader rejects a file with any `blockscompressed` bit set, as FTE does when built without zlib; reading compressed tables would add a decompressor for a mode that FTEQCC's default settings do not produce (`compressoutput` is zero-initialised in `qccmain.c`).
`ofsfiles` and the type table carry no information the engine needs to run the program; a reader keeps their offsets and counts and does not decode them.
The version 7 header is followed by the same six tables as version 6, and PROGS-15 applies to them; opcodes above 65 and type numbers above 7 are FTE extensions that the vanilla VM does not execute.
When `ofsfiles` is not 0, it is the offset of an i32 count followed by that many 144-byte embedded file records (`includeddatafile_t`, read by `PR_TestRecompile`):

When `ofs_types` is not 0, it is the offset of `numtypes` 28-byte type records (`typeinfo_t`): seven i32 fields `type`, `next`, `aux_type`, `num_parms`, `ofs`, `size` and `name`, the last a string reference. FTEQCC at the pinned commit never writes the table (`types` is always false in `WriteData`).
